::: {.dropcap}
\"Some trees bear no fruit,\" she said, her voice hinting at the rhythms of Creole. It was my first class at the women\'s shelter, and the organization\'s suggested icebreaker---asking how the students were like trees---felt hopelessly out of place. I was quiet for a few moments---no words are needed to recognize when one attests to their suffering. It required no explanation, no cheerful spin. Some burdens leave no room for flowering.
:::

Years later, I stumbled upon a classic story while reading an essay by Thoreau. He claims it comes from the \"Gulistan,\" penned by Persian poet Saadi of Shiraz nearly eight centuries ago. It tells of a wise man being questioned about the cypress tree, that evergreen giant that offers only the gift of itself, never bearing fruit. Why name it \'azad,\' the Farsi word for \'free,\' when it holds no sweetness for the world to taste?

The wise man answered, \"Other trees rise and fall with the seasons, but the cypress stands alone. Its freedom lies in needing nothing, not even the praise of fruitfulness. If fortune blesses you, be generous. But if fortune strips you bare, be like the cypress: unchanging even in the harshest wind.\"

The barrenness my student spoke of is a world apart from the one alluded to by the poet. The cypress of the rose garden symbolizes an ideal. But for immigrant women trapped within cycles of homelessness and poverty, the freedom to \'need nothing\' is a luxury they cannot afford. Survival itself becomes an elusive fruit, forever out of reach for those denied the basic necessities of life and the sanctuary of safety.

The virtues we so often extol -- detachment, resilience -- ring hollow in the presence of such suffering. What good is the wisdom of the cypress when its shade offers no shelter to those most in need? What use is resilience when it is forced upon the vulnerable, not chosen freely?

For the soul laid bare by the lash of circumstance, freedom may feel like an elusive dream. The heart that beats to the rhythm of a double consciousness, forever caught between the yearning for self-realization and the bitter knowledge of a society that has deemed them less than human, may find limited solace in the cypress\'s detached grandeur.

A tree, after all, is not meant to stand alone, but to be part of a forest, where its roots intertwine with those of its neighbors. The forest persists through storms, while the solitary tree perishes. The existence of each tree depends on the forest, just as the forest depends on each tree. There can be no forest when its trees are left to wither and die. And so it is with our communities -- if we fail to extend our roots and branches to those in need, if we turn a blind eye to the plight of others, our society will decay. 

It is worth mentioning, as this point is easily confused, that I am not discounting the power of individual agency. Remarkable people have clawed their way from the depths of circumstance into the good life, emboldened by their own cultivated minds. But if we focus solely on these exceptional cases, these rare triumphs over adversity, we risk obscuring the systemic failings within our communities that make such victories so rare in the first place.  

Reality is indifferent, brutal, and cruel, yet nature\'s design is one of interdependence. Just as the health of the individual tree is inextricably linked to the health of the forest, so too is the health of the forest dependent on the quality of the soil in which it grows. The fact that millions of Americans will suffer for no fault of their own should prompt us to examine the ground in which we are rooted.  

Our minds, beliefs, and sense of self have all been shaped by the conditions in which we are embedded. To truly understand ourselves and our society, we must be willing to look within and confront the poisons that lurk there. The same vices that plague our collective consciousness -- greed, ignorance, apathy -- also reside within us. They manifest in our worship of individualism despite our desolate sense of loneliness, our obsessive pursuit of material wealth, and our neglect of the soul. If our society is to prosper, we must first heal the earth beneath our feet.

Freedom, true freedom, is not a gift bestowed upon us by chance or circumstance. It is a harvest that must be sown and reaped with each generation. When the privileged few join hands with the disenfranchised many, when the scholar collaborates as equals with the laborer toward their common emancipation, can the seeds of liberation finally bear the fruit of freedom.
